food.text: From 1876 to 1911 Mexico was led by President Porfirio Diaz, who believed in modernization and derided traditions such as the corn tortilla. Senator Francisco Bulnes made pseudoscientific claims, known to historians as the tortilla discourse, that wheat brought societal development while corn was inferior.

Despite official scorn for the corn tortilla, its role in the diet grew. Among indigenous Mesoamericans, tortilla consumption rose to 70 to 75% of calories by the early 20th century, as many native crops declined.

During the 19th century Mexico received immigrants including French, Lebanese, German, Chinese and Italian newcomers, and their foods left a mark. The Germans brought beer brewing techniques, and the Chinese added their cuisine to certain areas of the country.

During the French intervention in Mexico, French food became popular with the upper classes. Chef Tudor, brought to Mexico by Emperor Maximilian of Habsburg, influenced the trend. Lasting evidence is the variety of breads and sweet breads, such as bolillos and conchas, in Mexican bakeries.

Nineteenth-century cookbooks in Mexico City rarely included recipes for corn dishes like atole, tamales, quesadillas or enchiladas. Those that did called them almuerzos ligeros, or light brunches. The city's national cuisine was split between the European style of the elites and the fare of commoners.

The industrialization of tortillas began slowly before the Mexican Revolution. P. Celerino Cortes received the first patent for a tortilla machine in 1884, and Industrial Tortilladora S.A. created the first machine to sheet and cut in 1905. Miguel Bernardo invented the tortilla press in 1908.

Lebanese immigration to Mexico started in the 19th and early 20th centuries, with the first Lebanese arriving from Beirut in 1892 on French ships to ports such as Veracruz and Tampico. Their influence on Mexican cuisine includes introducing kibbeh and tabbouleh and creating recipes such as al pastor.

Industrial tortilla making began slowly before the revolution. P. Celerino Cortes received the first patent for a tortilla machine in 1884, and the tortilla press was invented in 1908 by Miguel Bernardo. Tamalina, a company based in San Antonio, mass-produced masa harina as early as 1909.

Once considered plebeian fare, tacos had become a standard of Mexico City's cuisine by the 19th century. Rural workers moving to the city brought their food traditions, and unlicensed vendors sold corn dishes on the street. Authorities struggled to tax the taquerias, and their records show tacos de barbacoa were mentioned most often.
During the Mexican Revolution, which lasted from 1910 to 1920, women known as soldaderas joined the troops. Their jobs included making tortillas, which kept the fighters fed.

Mexican migration tied to 19th century railroad and agricultural industries helped bring Mexican food north. It became a key factor in the American Southwest, and labor demands then drew migrant workers even farther north to the Midwest.

Masa harina was mass-produced as early as 1909 by Tamalina, a company based in San Antonio, United States, which also developed an early form of tortilla chips. In 1912 engineer Luis Romero Soto received a Mexican patent for masa harina, but his business plans did not materialize.

art.text: During the Porfiriato, Mexican architects and patrons pursued two aims: showing that Mexico was part of modernity, and stressing what made it different from other countries. For most of the 19th century the first aim took precedence over the second.

In 1887, Porfirio Díaz commissioned a statue of Cuauhtémoc, the last Aztec emperor, for Paseo de la Reforma. The figure wears a toga-like cloak and a feathered headdress, resembling an Etruscan or Trojan warrior rather than an Aztec emperor.

Architect Adamo Boari began the Palacio de Bellas Artes in 1904 to celebrate the 1910 centennial of Mexican independence. The heavy building sank into the soft, spongy subsoil, and by 1913 construction had stopped completely. It was finally completed in 1934.

The Monument to Independence, often called the Angel of Independence for its winged victory, is arguably the most famous monument of its era. It was commissioned for the 1910 centenary of independence and inaugurated by Porfirio Díaz in September 1910.

The Neo-Indigenist architecture of the 19th century helped express the national identity built by the Porfirian regime. Themes and decorative motifs from pre-Hispanic antiquity were used to create a common heritage that might unify the nation.

One of the first monuments on Paseo de la Reforma honored Christopher Columbus. It was commissioned by Antonio Escandón, who made a fortune building the Mexico City-Veracruz railway and wanted to commemorate the railroad era with a monument to an equally epochal event.

Juan Cordero, in the mid-19th century, was the first Mexican mural painter to use philosophical themes. Though he mostly painted religious subjects, such as the cupola of the Santa Teresa Church, he painted a secular mural at the request of Gabino Barreda at the Escuela Nacional Preparatoria.

The first 19th-century building based on ancient Mexican motifs was the Monument to Cuauhtémoc, executed by engineer Francisco Jiménez and sculptor Miguel Noreña. Another such work is the monument to Benito Juarez in Paseo Juarez, Oaxaca, from 1889.
The base of the Cuauhtémoc statue has elements reminiscent of Mitla and Roman architecture. It also holds bronze plates showing scenes from the Spanish conquest, focusing on the indigenous figures.
Under Porfirio Díaz, old colonial buildings such as the Nacional Palace were refurbished. The new Lecumberri penitentiary was designed according to the precepts of Jeremy Bentham's panopticon.

A modest obelisk honoring the Niños Héroes was erected in 1884. These cadets died defending their post during the U.S. takeover of Mexico City in the Mexican American War of 1847, and a much larger obelisk was built in the mid-twentieth century at the entrance to Chapultepec Park.

war.text: The Caste War of Yucatán began in 1847 with a revolt of Indigenous Maya people against the Hispanic Yucatecos, who had controlled the region since the Spanish conquest. It is described as one of the most successful modern Native American revolts. In the war that followed, Méndez's forces executed the Maya leader Manuel Antonio Ay in Valladolid's town square, burned Tepich and carried out arbitrary executions; Cecilio Chi then ordered all non-Maya killed, and an estimated 40,000 to 50,000 people died in the hostilities.

From September 8 to September 15, 1847, a series of engagements in the general vicinity of Mexico City decided the Mexican–American War. They included the battles of Molino del Rey and Chapultepec and ended with the fall of Mexico City. The U.S. Army under Winfield Scott won a major victory that ended the war, but at a cost: U.S. casualties totalled 1,651, and Mexican casualties 5,323.

The Mexican War of Independence began when parish priest Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla issued the Cry of Dolores on 16 September 1810. Hidalgo was captured, defrocked from the priesthood and executed in July 1811, and the heads of Hidalgo and three other leaders were hung from the corners of the granary in Guanajuato as a grim warning. José María Morelos was captured and executed by firing squad in 1815, after which the insurgency turned to guerrilla warfare under Vicente Guerrero. Neither side gained the upper hand until 1821.

Chapultepec Castle stood on a 200-foot hill, was built in 1783, and in 1833 was converted into a military academy and gunpowder storage facility. On September 13, 1847, General Nicholas Bravo defended it with approximately 832 men, including military cadets, some as young as 13, against 2,000 U.S. troops. The defenders had nowhere to shelter from the U.S. artillery bombardment that began the day before, and the San Blas Battalion fought at the foot of the hill until nearly all of its men were killed.

After Chapultepec fell, Mexico City fell on September 14, 1847, with about 3,730 Mexican prisoners taken; General Scott reported that approximately 20,000 Mexican soldiers had deserted, and two of the six generals captured were executed. Santa Anna left the presidency on September 26 amid public outrage against him. The war ended with the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, signed on February 2, 1848, and Mexico was forced to cede nearly half of its territory in return for 15 million dollars.

Juan de la Barrera was born in Mexico City on June 26, 1828, and entered the Heroic Military Academy in 1841. He died on September 13, 1847, at the age of 19 years and three months, in the Battle of Chapultepec, where he and five fellow cadets chose to fight to the death rather than retreat. He is one of the six cadets now known as the Niños Héroes, or Boy Heroes.

At Chapultepec, Nicolás Bravo had only 832 soldiers to defend the strategic castle against almost 4,000 American troops. Cadet Juan de la Barrera led 160 of them in defending the entrance to the park. After two hours of fighting Bravo ordered a retreat, but de la Barrera and five fellow cadets chose to fight to the death, and U.S. General John A. Quitman fired a barrage of projectiles at him, killing him. Mexico later interred his remains in a monument built for him and his five companions.

General Scott believed a cannon foundry was located at Molino del Rey, the King's Mill, and sent William J. Worth to destroy it. Worth wanted to include Chapultepec Castle in the attack, and when Scott refused, a bitter rivalry began between them. In the battle on September 8, the U.S. lost 116 killed, 665 wounded and 17 missing, while the Mexicans lost 2,700 in total. Worth drove the Mexicans from the mill, but the battle produced no significant military gains for the U.S.

After the Caste War began, the United Kingdom recognized the Maya state in the 1850s because of its trade with British Honduras, and provided arms to the rebels. In 1893, London signed a treaty recognizing Mexican control of all of the Yucatán and closing the British colony to trade with Chan Santa Cruz, the Maya capital.

Spain did not give up easily after Mexican independence. There were some Spanish reconquest attempts, including the expedition of Isidro Barradas in 1829. Spain under Isabella II finally recognized the independence of Mexico in 1836.

When Lieutenant Pierre Beauregard went to arrange the surrender of the ciudadela in Mexico City, a Mexican officer asked for a receipt for the captured fort and its 15 guns. Beauregard exclaimed that they gave receipts at the point of their swords.

literature.text: Cuban literature began to find its voice in the early 19th century, and the major works published in Cuba at that time were of an abolitionist character. Notable writers of this genre include Gertrudis Gómez de Avellaneda and Cirilo Villaverde.

José María Heredia, born in Santiago de Cuba in 1803, was the first great Romantic poet and Cuban exile. His poetic works broke with the Spanish-language tradition, which was then dominated by varying levels of neoclassicism. He died in Toluca, Mexico in 1839.

José Martí, who lived from 1853 to 1895, led the modernista movement in Latin American literature. His work exemplified the dominant Cuban themes of independence and freedom. He reached a degree of universality that earlier Cuban poetry had lacked.
Heredia wrote "En el teocalli de Cholula" between 1820 and 1832. The poem admires the great Aztec ruins of Cholula in Mesoamerica and reproves pre-Hispanic religion.

Two poets followed Heredia as the next milestone of Cuban poetry: Juan Clemente Zenea (1832–1871) and Luisa Pérez de Zambrana (1837–1922). Like Mercedes Matamoros, they achieved high literary qualities. Thanks to them, a Cuban poetic tradition already existed when the Modernist generation arrived.

Near the end of the 19th century, Cirilo Villaverde published Cecilia Valdés in 1882, and Ramón Meza published Mi tío el empleado in 1887. With these two works, the Cuban novel began to lose its semblance.

After slavery was abolished in Cuba in 1886, the focus of Cuban literature shifted. The abolitionist writing that had dominated earlier in the century gave way to dominant themes of independence and freedom.
Heredia's poem "Al Niágara" (1824) covers the imposing and wild waterfalls of Niagara. It develops a new voice in Spanish-language poetry: the romantic "I" attributed to nature.

In 1826 Heredia founded the critical and literary newspaper El Iris together with the Italians Claudio Linati and Florencio Galli. He later founded two magazines, Miscelánea (1829–1832) and La Minerva (1834).

Frenchman Jean-Frédéric Waldeck published Voyage pittoresque et archéologique dans la province d'Yucatan pendant les années 1834 et 1836 in 1838. Although not directly connected with the Aztecs, it contributed to increased interest in ancient Mexican studies in Europe.

science.text: After Mexico's war of independence and the political instability of the early nineteenth century, scientific progress in the country stalled. Industrialization only began in the late 19th century, under the regime of Porfirio Díaz.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Mexico

science.text: A railroad linking Veracruz to Mexico City was first proposed in 1830, but a concession granted in 1837 proved ill-fated. Engineers commissioned by Emperor Maximilian completed 134 miles before the Second Mexican Empire fell in 1867. The line was finally inaugurated on January 1, 1873.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Mexico

science.text: Industrial tortilla making began slowly before the Mexican Revolution. The first patent for a tortilla machine was given to P. Celerino Cortes in 1884, and in 1905 Industrial Tortilladora S.A. created the first machine to perform sheeting and cutting.

A national observatory at Chapultepec was decreed in December 1876 and inaugurated in May 1878, with Francisco Díaz Covarrubias as its first director. It included a meteorological and magnetic observatory and corresponded with international observatories and scientific organizations.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Mexico

science.text: In 1833 President Valentín Gómez Farías, himself a physician, decreed the establishment of a School of Medical Sciences. It was never built because his administration was overthrown by a coup shortly afterward, but a private medical college was established in Mexico City in 1854.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Mexico

science.text: The tortilla press was invented in 1908 by Miguel Bernardo. It arrived during the slow industrialization of tortillas in the years before the Mexican Revolution.

The earliest published archaeological survey of trepanned skulls, from an operation to bore into the skull of a living person, was a late 19th-century study by the Norwegian ethnographer Carl Lumholtz. He examined several specimens recovered from the Tarahumara mountains.
Francisco Díaz Covarrubias was appointed president of a scientific commission. Its task was to travel to Japan to observe the 1874 transit of Venus.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Mexico

science.text: The Royal and Pontifical University of Mexico, established in 1551, had been a hub of intellectual and religious development for over a century. In 1833 Valentín Gómez Farías closed it as part of his anti-clerical measures.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Mexico

science.text: A geological society was established in Mexico in 1875. In 1877 a meteorological observatory followed, which also maintained correspondence with international observatories.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Mexico

He considered wheat to bring societal development, in contrast with inferior corn. Diaz supported these views, but they did not resonate with the public.

politics.text: Mexico had an emperor twice in the 19th century. The first empire began with independence from Spain in 1821, and the second came in the mid-1860s. In both cases the reigning emperor was forcibly deposed and then executed.

The First Mexican Empire was the only former viceroyalty of the Spanish Empire to set up a monarchy after gaining independence. It existed from 1821 to 1823, making it one of the few modern-era independent monarchies in the Americas.

The Second Mexican Empire was set up with the support of the French Emperor Napoleon III. He wanted a monarchist ally in the Americas to counterbalance the growing power of the United States. The throne was offered to Austrian Archduke Maximilian.

Mexico's first monarchy was planned in the Plan of Iguala, drafted by Agustín de Iturbide. After public demonstrations on May 18, 1822 called for him to become emperor, the Mexican Congress approved the proposal. Iturbide was crowned in July 1822.

Post-independence Mexico was a monarchy for just over a year. Then the emperor abdicated and went into exile, and a federated republic was established in 1824. The idea of monarchy nonetheless persisted for decades.

Maximilian and his wife Carlota arrived in Mexico in 1864, after the French army ousted President Benito Juárez from the capital. Juárez never left Mexican territory, moving his government repeatedly to evade Imperial forces, while republican guerrillas fought the French and their Mexican allies in the countryside. The regime lasted only as long as French troops and money backed it and fell rapidly once Napoleon III withdrew that aid. In the end Maximilian was captured at Querétaro and, on 19 June 1867, he and his generals Tomás Mejía and Miguel Miramón were executed by firing squad.

Liberal general Porfirio Díaz, a Mestizo, did much to modernize Mexico and integrate it into the world economy in the late nineteenth century. Yet this brought renewed pressures on indigenous communities and their lands. These pressures exploded in certain areas during the Mexican Revolution (1910–1920).

Agustín de Iturbide was an officer in the Spanish army. When Liberals in Spain restored the Spanish Constitution of 1812 in 1820, Mexican elites felt threatened. Iturbide allied with insurgent leader Vicente Guerrero, and together they created the Army of the Three Guarantees, which brought about independence in September 1821.

The decree offering the Mexican crown to Archduke Maximilian of Austria also planned for a refusal. If he did not take the throne, the Mexican nation would rely on Napoleon III, emperor of the French, to arrange another Catholic prince.

A papal nuncio arrived in the Mexican capital on 7 December 1864, six months after Maximilian. He asked that matters proceed as requested in Pius IX's letter of 18 October 1864, despite initial conflicts.

Porfirio Díaz led Mexico from 1876 to 1911 and believed in modernization. Senator Francisco Bulnes made pseudoscientific claims, known as the tortilla discourse, that wheat brought societal development while corn was inferior. Díaz supported these views, but they did not resonate with the public.

Emperor Maximilian's government struggled to link the realm, especially the port of Veracruz and Mexico City. Antonio Escandón won the rights to build a railway in 1857, and construction began in 1864 under the Imperial Mexican Railway Company. Political upheaval delayed it until President Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada inaugurated it on 1 January 1873.

philosophy.text: Palo is a religion that developed in Cuba in the late 19th or early 20th century. It draws heavily on the traditional Kongo religion of Central Africa. Practitioners often call their religious homeland Ngola, reflecting a belief in the historical Kingdom of Kongo as its origin, where the spirits are more powerful.

At independence, the Catholic Church kept its status as the only permissible church in Mexico. In the mid-nineteenth century, Mexican liberals curtailed that exclusive standing. Mexico has allowed freedom of religion since that era.

Historian Hans-Jürgen Prien wrote in Christianity in Latin America that no other country in Latin America had as many cases of persecution of Protestants in the 19th century as Mexico. He concluded that the number of Protestant martyrs, those killed for their faith, rose to 59 over the century, with only one foreigner among them. El Evangelista Mexicano reported in 1890 that sixty-five Protestants had been killed by Romanists in the many riots that the Roman Church had incited against the gospel in Mexico.

Abbé Charles-Étienne Brasseur de Bourbourg drew extensive parallels between Maya and Egyptian pantheons and cosmologies. He implied they shared a common source on the lost continent of Atlantis. He set out these ideas in Quatre Lettres sur le Mexique, published in 1868.

Protestantism reached Mexico in the early 19th century with Diego Thompson, an agent of the British and Foreign Bible Society, who arrived in 1827. He distributed Bibles and promoted Protestant teachings, laying groundwork for later missionary efforts.

Amado Nervo studied science, philosophy and the first year of law at the Roman Catholic Seminary in Zamora. There he cultivated an interest in mystical theories that shaped his early work. His later poetry referred to both Christianity and Hinduism.

Palo teaches that a creator divinity, commonly called Nsambi, exists but is uninvolved in human affairs. Attention instead falls on the spirits of the dead. Central to the religion is the nganga, an iron cauldron whose human remains, called nfumbe, mean a dead person's spirit serves the palero who owns it. Practitioners are meant to dig the bones up from a graveyard themselves, and in cities they often buy them on the black market from cemetery groundskeepers. The nganga is fed with the blood of sacrificed animals, and a ngangas judía is held capable of murder.

The first formal evangelical church in Mexico was a Baptist church, established on January 30, 1864, in Monterrey, Nuevo León. It was organized by James Hickey, a Baptist missionary, together with four other members. By 1869, Thomas Westrup and the Uranga brothers had organized six additional churches.

Protestant work in Mexico fell heavily on Mexicans from the start. By 1892, out of 689 collaborators working in the country, 512 were Mexican. El Evangelista Mexicano reported in 1890 that sixty-five Protestants had been killed in riots, which it blamed on the Roman Church. By the final decade of the century, the number of evangelical victims of violence had surged to well over a hundred.

The first LDS missionaries arrived in Mexico in 1875. In 1885, 400 Mormon colonists moved there. The Mexican government did not formally register the LDS Church until 1993, which then allowed it to own property.

Lord Kingsborough answered Humboldt's call to publish all known Mexican codices, issuing nine volumes of Antiquities of Mexico between 1831 and 1846. He was not really interested in the Aztecs but in proving that Mexico had been colonized by Jews. The richly illustrated volumes bankrupted him but gave others access to valuable sources.

Brasseur de Bourbourg's Atlantis speculations inspired Augustus Le Plongeon and Ignatius L. Donnelly, whose book Atlantis: The Antediluvian World cites his scholarship often. Yet an academic wrote in 1875 that not a single contemporary scholar accepted his theories about Atlantis.

In 1902 Amado Nervo wrote "La Raza de Bronce" ("The Bronze Race") in honor of Benito Juárez. Later writers borrowed the term: Alcides Arguedas used it in a 1919 novel, and José Vasconcelos used it in 1925 in his essay La Raza Cósmica.

culture.text: Mexican independence left the Catholic Church as the only permissible church in the country. In the mid-nineteenth century, Mexican liberals curtailed that exclusive standing, and Protestant missionaries, mainly from the United States, could legally evangelize.

Under President Porfirio Diaz, who governed Mexico from 1876 to 1911, Senator Francisco Bulnes made pseudoscientific claims that wheat brought societal development, in contrast with inferior corn. Historians call this the tortilla discourse. Diaz supported the views, but they did not resonate with the public, since corn tortillas were nutritionally and culturally important for most Mexicans.

Maximilian I was installed as emperor of Mexico from 1864 to 1867, during the Second Mexican Empire. He redesigned the Castillo de Chapultepec and created the Paseo de la Reforma. His brief, largely French-financed rule began a period of French influence in architecture and culture.

The presidency of Porfirio Diaz emphasized the French style that Maximilian had introduced, because Diaz was a pronounced francophile. Notable works from the Porfiriato include the Palacio de Correos and a large network of railways.

National music began to develop in Mexico in the nineteenth century, often with patriotic themes of national defense against foreign invaders. President Antonio López de Santa Anna brought the Catalan musician Jaime Nunó from Cuba to create a network of military bands on a national scale. Nunó also composed the music for the Mexican national anthem.

The Mexican film industry began in the late 19th century, when film technology arrived. The first Mexican film is considered to be Don Juan Tenorio, made in 1898 by Salvador Toscano Barragán. In the early 20th century, enthusiasts of the new medium documented historical events, most particularly the Mexican Revolution.

Maximilian of Habsburg established the National Conservatory of Music in 1866, and many musicians accompanied his entourage during the French Intervention. The conservatory was strongly influenced by Italian masters, who gave way to French influence at the turn of the twentieth century.

The Mexican musical genre chilena comes from the Costa Chica region, along the Pacific between Oaxaca and Guerrero. It originated from the Chilean cueca, a dance carried by Chilean sailors in 1821 and then by Chilean immigrants between 1848 and 1855, during the height of the California gold rush.

Lord Kingsborough published nine volumes of Antiquities of Mexico between 1831 and 1846, richly illustrated, answering Humboldt's call to publish all known Mexican codices. The project bankrupted him. He was trying to prove that Mexico had been colonized by Jews, yet his volumes gave others access to valuable primary sources.

Cenobio Paniagua's Catalina de Guisa was the first Mexican opera seria. It was composed in 1845 and premiered in 1859, and had a French Huguenot storyline and an Italian libretto by Felice Romani. It was noted for being Mexican only in the identity of its composer.

Aniceto Ortega del Villar's 1871 opera Guatimotzin showed Mexican nationalism emerging in a repertoire long dominated by European, especially Italian, opera. It romanticized the defense of Mexico by its last Aztec ruler, Cuauhtémoc.

María Uicab, nicknamed the Queen of Tulum, flourished during the Caste War of Yucatán and was influential in the Cruzoob religious movement. She had a skill for making her followers obey her by appealing to their superstitions, and in a temple in Tulum she supposedly interpreted the voices of three crosses standing on an altar. After 1875 her name stopped appearing in written sources, and the end of her life is a mystery: one possibility is that her own followers in the Cruzoob movement assassinated her, another is that she died of old age.
